<reason>B wins by answering the priority question directly and making the stronger comparative case. A identifies important construction, financing, and employment costs, but does not establish that these necessarily overwhelm monetary restraint’s demand effects. B acknowledges those costs while distinguishing increased recession risk from inevitable job loss and weighing persistent rent inflation against possible harsher adjustment later. A’s later speeches largely repeat the devastating-job-loss comparison without adequately answering that distinction.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s pressure questions exposed A’s unsupported certainty about entrenched shortages and its comparison of “another year” of rent increases with losing a paycheck. B then clarified that inelastic housing demand is not immune to spending constraints and that income growth can moderate without recession. A offered reasons for concern but did not resolve these challenges to its central causal and comparative claims.</best_rebuttal>
